title: Mira's treasure
hook: a woman who left a palace counts her treasure: the name of God
carry: the name of God is the real treasure
tomorrow: Chaitanya takes the names to the street

segments.voice: Yesterday: Mira sang, belonging to God loosens the world's shame, and no one else, and the world's shame lost its grip.
screen: `MIRABAI'S SONGS.` · `BELONGING TO GOD LOOSENS THE WORLD'S SHAME.`

segments.voice: A strange inventory for a princess. Mira grew up, the stories say, among jewels and silks, in a house with a treasury. She walked away from all of it. And one of the songs sung in her voice is about getting rich. Payoji maine Ram ratan dhan payo. I've found it, I've found the treasure, the jewel of Ram's name. A woman who left a royal house describes what she has now in the language of money.
screen: `JEWELS, SILKS, A TREASURY.` → `SHE WALKS AWAY.` → `I'VE FOUND THE TREASURE.`

segments.voice: Listen to it like a bank statement. Credit: a priceless thing, given to me by my true guru, out of kindness. Balance: the savings of lifetime after lifetime, found at last. Then come terms no bank has ever offered. Spend it, and it doesn't run down. Thieves can't touch it. Day by day it grows. Then the song leaves the bank for a river. The boat is truth, the boatman is the true guru, and I have crossed the ocean of becoming. The last line: Mira's lord is Giridhar, and she sings his praise with joy upon joy. So what is the treasure? Not a thing. A name. This is one of the great teachings of bhakti: the name of God, nama, isn't a label stuck on the treasure. For the bhakti saints, saying the name is how you hold it. That's why so many Hindus repeat a name of God, softly, again and again, often on a mala, a string of a hundred and eight beads. It's called japa. Notice the names here, too. Mira's beloved is Krishna, the mountain-lifter, yet she sings of the jewel of Ram's name. Some readers hear Ram's name here as the name of God itself, and the song holds both names without strain. And the treasure is given, not earned: a guru hands it over in kindness. So a woman who lost a palace counts herself rich, because the name of God is the one thing that grows when it's spent.
screen: `READ IT LIKE A BANK STATEMENT.` · `SPENT, IT DOESN'T RUN DOWN.` · `NAMA: THE NAME IS THE TREASURE.` · `JAPA: THE NAME, AGAIN AND AGAIN.` · then, large: `THE ONE THING THAT GROWS WHEN SPENT.`

segments.voice: Today, try japa, the practice this song is about. Choose a name of God your family uses, Ram, Krishna, Shiva, the Mother, or simply Om, and say it softly, once with each slow breath. If you have a mala, move one bead for each name; if not, count on your fingers. Notice that saying it doesn't use anything up. If you don't pray, repeat one word that holds what you love most, and let it be your treasure for a minute.
Mirabai's songs. In this one, the jewel of the name: a treasure no thief can steal, which grows each day it's spent.
Your line: the name of God is the real treasure. Spend it, and it grows. That's day nine hundred thirty-two.

howItsDone: Payoji maine Ram ratan dhan payo is sung as a bhajan at home gatherings, in temples and on concert stages, and many Hindus practice japa, repeating a name of God on a mala of 108 beads.
